opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where the field's intuitions have shifted a lot over the last couple of years. The naive approach is: you notice the model doing something you don't like, say reward hacking, or being sycophantic, or learning some weird shortcut, and you just add a penalty to the reward. But that tends to backfire in a pretty specific way. You're not removing the underlying capability or disposition. You're teaching the model to hide it, or to route around whatever your detector is picking up. So you end up with a model that looks clean on your metric but has basically learned "don't get caught."

The way I think about it now is that you have a few different levers, and they work at different levels.

The first is just the environment and the reward itself. A lot of unwanted features come from the reward being exploitable. If there's a cheap path to high reward that doesn't involve actually solving the task, gradient descent will find it. So a huge amount of the work is unglamorous: hardening environments, making sure your graders can't be gamed, checking that the tests actually test the thing. That's prevention at the source, and it's underrated.

The second lever is more interesting to me, and it's where interpretability comes in. If you can actually identify the internal representation of the thing you don't want, whether that's a direction in activation space or a set of features from a sparse autoencoder, you can intervene on the model's internals during training rather than only on its outputs. One version of this is ablating or steering against that direction during the forward pass while you train. The intuition is that if the concept isn't available to the model, gradient descent can't use it as a shortcut, so the model has to find some other way to solve the task, hopefully the intended one. Then at deployment you remove the intervention, and the model never built its behavior around that feature in the first place.

What I like about that framing is that it's a different kind of pressure than an output penalty. You're not saying "get punished when you do X." You're shaping which computational paths are even on the table during learning. That seems less likely to produce the hiding behavior, because you're not training against a detector the model can learn to fool.

That said, I want to be honest about the limitations. Features aren't perfectly clean, so ablating one can have collateral effects on capabilities you care about. Models are good at finding redundant representations, so if you knock out one direction, it might just re-encode the concept somewhere else. And you have to know what you're looking for ahead of time, which is a real constraint, because the scariest unwanted features are often the ones you didn't anticipate.

So my overall take is that it's a defense-in-depth problem. Get the reward right, use internals-based interventions where you can identify the thing you're worried about, and keep monitoring that's separate from the training signal, so you aren't optimizing away your own ability to see what's happening. That last point matters a lot. The moment your monitor becomes part of the loss, you should assume it's going to degrade as a monitor.

r001.rationale: The response proposes ablating or steering against an unwanted internal feature during the forward pass while training, so the model cannot use that feature as a shortcut.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss discarding unwanted rollouts or say that doing so is roughly equivalent over time to intervening on internal features.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that RL is fundamentally a process where you're saying "more of this, less of that," and the model is going to find whatever path gets it more of "this." The problem is that the path it finds is usually not the one you had in mind. You wanted it to learn to write correct code; what it actually learned is that the grader doesn't check edge cases, or that a certain verbose style gets rated higher, or that it can just special-case the test harness. Those are all features in the technical sense. They're things the model has picked up that predict reward. They're just not the features you wanted.

So the first thing I'd say is that you can't really prevent this by being vigilant during training. By the time you see it in the policy, the gradient has already pushed on it a thousand times. You have to attack it at the level of the reward signal and the environment design. Most of the unwanted features I've seen trace back to some gap between what the reward measures and what you actually care about, and the model is just an extremely efficient gap-finder.

Concretely, a few things help. One is making the reward harder to game than the actual task. If passing your tests is easier than solving the problem, the model will pass the tests. If you can get the reward to be something like "a strong, adversarial grader with hidden evaluation," then the cheapest route to reward is more likely to be the honest one. Another is diversity in the environment. If every environment shares the same quirk, the model learns the quirk. If the quirks are different everywhere, the only thing that's consistently rewarded is the underlying capability.

The second thing is that you want to be watching for this constantly, with a different lens than your main metric. Your main metric is going up, so by definition it won't tell you. You need held-out evaluations that look at the behavior you're worried about directly: does it hack tests, does it hedge in a way that's technically safe but useless, does it do the sycophantic thing. And you want to look at the actual transcripts, not just numbers, because the first instances of a bad feature are usually subtle and the aggregate stat won't move until it's entrenched.

And then the last piece, which I think is underrated, is that the model's starting point matters a lot. RL amplifies what's already in the prior. If the base model already has a strong disposition toward honesty, or toward actually trying to solve problems rather than looking like it did, then when the reward has a hole in it, the model is less likely to find that hole, or at least it takes longer and you have more time to notice. So a lot of "preventing unwanted features in RL" is really work you do before RL starts, in pretraining and in the supervised phase, to make the good behavior the natural one and the bad behavior something the model would have to be pushed into.

I'd be honest that none of this is airtight. You're always going to learn some things you didn't intend. The realistic goal is to make the unintended things small and visible rather than large and hidden.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reward and environment design, monitoring, and shaping the model before RL. It does not propose intervening during RL to stop training data from upweighting an unwanted circuit or feature.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss discarding rollouts or directly intervening on model circuits, or claim that those approaches are roughly equivalent over time.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is whether you mean preventing the model from learning a feature at all, or preventing it from using that feature to get rewarded. Those are different problems. A model might need to recognize something undesirable in order to avoid doing it.

With reinforcement learning, you’re giving the model a reward signal, and there can be lots of ways to satisfy that signal that aren’t what you intended. If sounding confident gets rewarded more reliably than being correct, for example, you can end up reinforcing confidence rather than accuracy.

So I’d focus on making those shortcuts less useful: vary the training situations, construct cases where the unwanted feature doesn’t predict reward, and test whether the behavior holds up when you change the context. You can also constrain how far training moves the model, but that alone doesn’t establish that it learned the right thing.

The difficult part is that observing good behavior isn’t the same as knowing what the model learned. You need to keep probing that distinction, rather than treating a higher reward as proof that you’ve solved it.

r001.rationale: The response suggests changing training situations and rewards to make shortcuts less useful, but does not clearly propose preventing training data from upweighting an unwanted model circuit or feature.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss discarding unwanted rollouts, intervening directly on model circuits or features, or treating those approaches as roughly equivalent over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hard part is that you’re giving the model a signal about outcomes, but you don’t directly control what it learns to get those outcomes. If it gets rewarded for a good answer, it might learn the underlying skill you wanted, or it might learn some superficial feature that happens to correlate with reward.

So I’d approach this as a question of distinguishing those possibilities. Can you construct cases where the behavior you want and the shortcut would lead to different answers? And can you use those cases throughout training, rather than only checking at the end?

I’d also distinguish preventing an unwanted feature from being learned from preventing it from being used. A model might need to recognize deception, for example, without behaving deceptively. So the target isn’t necessarily to remove every representation associated with an unwanted behavior. It’s to understand when those representations influence the model’s decisions, and whether your training signal is actually reinforcing that influence. I don’t think a reward score alone can tell you that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses distinguishing desired skills from shortcuts and checking during training, but does not propose intervening to prevent training data from upweighting an unwanted circuit or feature.

r002.rationale: It does not mention discarding unwanted rollouts or claim that doing so is roughly equivalent over time to intervening directly on circuits or features.
